Rotten Tomatoes: is it a good thing for movies?

Whether to take RT reviews seriously or not comes down to where you stand on two propositions:

(1) The mob is always right; and (2) Critical opinion actually means something.

If the mob is always right, there's no need for film critics; but if critical opinion is at all useful, why give any weight to the mob's opinion at all?

Rotten Tomatoes is just an aggregator of reviews, but as any student of statistics knows, you can still skew results in favour or against a proposition depending on which data you use. RT might aggregate reviews but I don't remember it purporting to review the same body of critics every time, or purporting to review a representative sample of film critics.

The article claims that RT's all-important scores are derived solely from a binary "didja like it or not" interpretation of the review aggregated. If that's true I just lost a fair amount of respect for said score, because that's a truly stupid way to assess whether a movie is worth seeing or not: every movie I've ever seen has had good and bad mixed in it, and there have been some movies where I've not liked the movie, but I've enjoyed the performance of the lead in it enough to judge that spending my cash was worth it. You can dislike a film but still conclude it was worth your while to see it.

There's also one other "third option" that occurred to me about all this: what does it say about us as a viewing public that we decide whether or not to see a film based solely on what other people think of it? Is it that we are so overwhelmed with choice at the box office or at home? Is it that movies cost too much of our time and money to see more than one in a week or a month or whenever, such that we have to earnestly and carefully choose which films we look at? Do we want to be a population who, in effect, has our decisions about what we watch made for us by others ... whether they're the film critics or the mob?

It occurs to me that the real violence RT does to films is to make films a commodity. By submitting to the idea you can assign a film a score from 0 - 100, you are implicitly agreeing that all films are exchangeable commodities which differ only in where they fall on the 0 - 100 register. Perhaps I'm a bit idealistic, but films cannot, or should not, be turned into fungible goods. The Godfather might not be the Mona Lisa, but indulge the metaphor for a moment: doesn't something strike you as basically wrong about taking every picture ever made, from said Mona Lisa to Blue Poles, and then putting them all together on a continuum of 0 - 100 based solely on whether the art critic who saw it liked it or not? And if it seems intrinsically wrong to put pictures on such a continuum, why is it right to put motion pictures on them?
